newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli minister says peace deal "mistake".
newsitem.headline: Israeli minister says peace deal "mistake".

text.p: Israel's internal security minister said on Friday the landmark 1993 peace deal with the PLO was a "fundamental mistake" and insisted Israel must hold half of the West Bank in a final accord with the Palestinians.

Avigdor Kahalani, seen as a moderate in the current government, labelled a "disaster" the fact the government had to try to implement a deal "it did not believe in" which was hammered out by a prior administration.

Kahalani's comments came a day after Palestinians were outraged over an Israeli newspaper report that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu planned to offer the PLO only about 40 percent of the West Bank at final negotiations.

Netanyahu held talks with an Egyptian peace envoy on Thursday on ways to revive peacemaking between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) that plunged into deep crisis in March when Israel began work on a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
"In large, it is about half of the West Bank that must be in Israeli hands in order to protect the interests we talked about earlier," Kahalani told Israel Radio.

Regarding the framework 1993 peace accord reached at Oslo between the PLO and Israel's previous, dovish government which set up Palestinian self-rule and set parameters for final peace talks, Kahalani said:
"I think the Oslo agreement, all the signing of that, was a fundamental mistake.

"I think it is a disaster from the point of view that this government must implement something that it does not believe in, and I think also the prior government, if it had to implement the Oslo agreement, would not have been able to."

The prior government, ousted in elections a year ago, handed over much of the Gaza Strip and seven West Bank cities to the PLO. Netanyahu, after months of acrimonious talks, handed over part of another town under a deal cut by the prior government.
More than two million Palestinians live in East Jerusalem, the rest of the West Bank and Gaza, captured by Israel in 1967.
Palestinians view settlement building in the areas, where they hope one day to establish an independent state, as pre-empting final negotiations.

Netanyahu's office said in a statement on Thursday that Egyptian envoy Osama al-Baz briefed Netanyahu on his meeting with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on Wednesday, adding that the talks were "positive".
The Palestinian reaction to the Haaretz newspaper report of a secret Netanyahu plan to hold onto 60 percent of the West Bank was anything but positive on Thursday.
"These numbers -- excuse the expression -- are political masturbation by the government of Israel," Arafat's adviser Ahmed Tibi told Israeli army radio.

Netanyahu acknowledged in radio interviews having ideas about a final deal and said they were discussed in his inner cabinet for the first time on Wednesday when the military presented its security assessments.
But he said: "I haven't shown anyone or drafted any map."
Tibi called the proposal published by Haaretz "a shot with automatic fire at the dying body of the Oslo accord...Benjamin Netanyahu is successfully destroying this process," he said.
